newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl says EMU criteria, deadline will be met.
newsitem.headline: Kohl says EMU criteria, deadline will be met.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, the main driving force behind European integration, said on Tuesday he was confident the terms and the deadline for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would be met.
"I am sure that we will achieve this goal," Kohl said at the launch of a book by Finance Minister Theo Waigel.
In the book, "Our future is called Europe", Waigel attempts to convince a sceptical German public to surrender their beloved mark in favour of the planned single European currency.
Its publication comes just as European nations enter the final straight in the race to whip their public budgets into shape to meet the conditions for entry to monetary union.
The budgetary conditions have proved the most challenging of a series of economic criteria laid down in the Maastricht Treaty which must be met by would-be EMU participants.
But Kohl made clear that the answer to the problems countries were facing in meeting these conditions by a 1997 deadline did not lie in changing the Maastricht goalposts.
"The criteria and the deadline are not open to discussion. Any change could endanger the entire project," Kohl said.

Buoyed by a weekend deal by European Union finance ministers which set broad terms for a "stability pact" to enforce budget discipline after the Euro's planned launch in 1999, Kohl said the "European train" was gathering steam.

Addressing innate German fears of hyperinflation, Kohl said he was sure the planned European central bank would be independent and oriented towards a stable monetary policy, making the future Euro as stable as the mark.
"For Germans, the Euro is not just any topic, it is the (most important) topic of the past 50 years. It is important very simply because it is about money," Kohl said.
The aim of Waigel's book was to provoke a domestic discussion that will create a broad basis of trust in the Euro among a majority of the German public.
He added he hoped the book would attract a wide readership. Finance Ministry officials said the first printing of the 58 mark ($38.35) book was 5,000 copies.
Waigel, at the same news conference, assured the chancellor the stability pact would have the necessary "bite" to keep participants toeing the line even after the start of EMU.

Germany's main concern is that the stability pact, conceived by Waigel and endorsed by finance ministers over the weekend, is armoured with clear definitions and penalties for those that relax their fiscal discipline.

"The rapid internationalisation of markets demands of Europe a common monetary policy and a coordinated economic policy," Waigel said. "When the business sector is thinking globally, the political sphere cannot deal just nationally."

European nations' efforts to align their economies in preparation for currency union have already had beneficial effects, Waigel said. Inflation, which raged at 13 percent in the 1980s, has been brought down to three percent, he noted.

Current Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, who has been at the helm of the fiecely-independent Bundesbank since 1993, was likely to be the first German governor at the European Central Bank Council, Waigel added.
But German niggling about the integration process reaches even Waigel's inner circle.

Former Bundesbank President Helmut Schlesinger, one of the contributors to Waigel's book, wrote that the government should not hold so firmly to the Maastricht requirement of keeping outstanding debt below 60 percent of gross domestic product.

The debt rule itself was in conflict with a second rule that annual public sector deficits be less than three percent of GDP, Schlesinger said, adding that even at that deficit level, overall debt would continue to grow. ($1=1.5124 Mark)
